newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 14.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. For further information on these articles or details of BMC's other international press and broadcast services call Simon McMillan on +44 (0)171 256 5130 or e-mail bmc.co@ft.com -- BT MAY DEMAND RESIGNATIONS AT MCI

Doug Maine, the finance director of US long-distance company MCI, and Tim Price, head of MCI's telecoms business, are expected to come under fire this week from top executives at British Telecoms concerning the American group's unexpected profit warning last Wednesday. BT will reportedly demand the resignation of the two MCI employees, and as a result Maine will no longer become finance director of Concert and Price will not assume responsibility of MCI's North American operations should the merger go ahead. -- PUBLIC SPENDING WATCHDOGS TO CHECK CAMELOT RECORDS

Heritage secretary Chris Smith is expected, before the end of July, to tighten regulations on Camelot, the operator of the National Lottery in Britain. Among Smith's new regime will be calls for punitive fines for breaches of license, and authorisation for the National Audit Office to see the Camelot's books. Smith is hoping the new plans will take attention away from the Labour party's manifesto pledge to run the lottery on a 'non-profit' basis as it now appears unlikely any group will take over the lottery on such a basis. -- BRUSSELS TRIES TO WIDEN WORKING TIME DIRECTIVE

The European Commission is seeking to extend the limits on working hours in the EU to include millions of junior doctors, transport and offshore workers and others. Current regulations that allow varying hours due to irregular work patterns in some industries have been labelled excessive by EU social affairs minister Padraig Flynn, who has called for limited exemptions in the future. A white paper to be forwarded to the commission on Tuesday will request that only 'mobile' workers -- such as offshore oil workers -- be exempt from the 48-hour week maximum. -- BRITAIN DOUBLES SHARE OF EU INWARD INVESTMENT

According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the UK received 40 percent of the inward directed investment reported by EU members in 1996 and has attracted larger inflows than any industrialised country except the US. Inflows to the UK rose from $22.8 billion 1995 to $32.8 billion, more than double those in France, the next country in the list. The Labour party has used the statistics to attack Tory claims that maintaining the UK's opt-out from the European social chapter was essential to attract inward investment. -- EU HOPEFULS WANT EMU START ON TIME

Central bankers and politicians from the five European states selected for EU expansion have announced they will continue with tough fiscal and monetary policies in order to qualify for both EU entry in the near future and EMU entry further down the line. Gyorgy Suranyi of the Hungarian National Bank said his country's greatest concern was that the EMU begin as scheduled as "any delay is likely to be for a decade rather than a few months", thus impacting on the country's EU entry negotiations. -- ICI SET FOR BULK CHEMICALS DEAL

Imperial Chemical Industries is expected some time this week to announce the sale of the majority of its industrial chemicals operations to DuPont, the US chemicals giant. The disposals at ICI, which may total up to two billion stg, mark the shift in focus at ICI from the bulk commodity chemicals area towards the higher margin specialty chemicals business. -- EXPANSION IN EUROPE SWELLS PRICE WATERHOUSE PARTNERS

UK Big Six accountancy firm Price Waterhouse will on Monday announce a six percent increase in its European customers to nearly 1,000 in total. The firm called the 256 percent increase in its audit and business services partners and 186 percent increase in tax and legal services 'staggering'. P&W is looking for its expansion to be seen in global terms, while it seeks to secure a share of the multinational cross-border market for business services. -- DAIRY SALES ROUND NEARS DEADLINE

Analysts have advised dairy companies to "stand back from the market" rather than decide how to participate in a new Milk Marque selling round. Milk Marque, the collector and distributor of about 14 million litres of milk daily in England and Wales, recently said it could not sell milk at current prices and reduced costs by 2p per litre to 2.5p, a price dairy companies said was still excessive. Milk Marque has now threatened to set up in processing in competition with dairy companies, thus reversing the 1994 deregulation of the milk market. -- LITTLEWOODS CLOSE TO DEAL ON STORES' SALE

Privately owned retail and pools group Littlewoods is reportedly close to reaching an agreement with another retailer that would result in the sale of 19 of its 135 high-street stores. A number of national retailers such as Boots, Tesco and Marks & Spencer have expressed interest in Littlewoods, which is looking to restructure its business with the aim of floating in two to three years. -- ENERGY GROUP TO RAISE 15M STG FOR RENEWABLE POWER

Renewable UK energy group Energy Power Resources is set to begin a 15 million stg fund-raising campaign this week, which will hand almost half of the group over to institutional investors. William Law, EPR co-founder and non-executive chairman, said that over the next few years, electricity generation from renewable resources "will become a major growth sector" and EPR is expected to become profitable by 2000 after recording pre-tax losses of 400,000 stg in the next two years. EPR is aiming for a 2002 stock market listing, when sales are expected to reach about 80 million stg.
